Welcome! I'm so glad you're joining me for this journey—a journey that goes beyond the surface of American neighborhoods, and pulls back the curtain on how the places we call home came to be divided, and why it still matters.
You know, segregation in our cities and suburbs wasn't just the result of chance or even just private prejudice. It was shaped—and enforced—by decisions made in government offices, at every level.
In Richard Rothstein's remarkable book, The Color of Law: A Forgotten History of How Our Government Segregated America, we get the undeniable evidence of how policies—housing laws, zoning rules, and federal, state, and local actions—wove lines of separation right into the fabric of our communities.
Together, we're going to unpack how redlining, discriminatory lending, and urban planning weren't just isolated events—they were part of a larger system that held back generations of Black Americans, limiting not only where people could live, but also their access to wealth, education, and health.
As we explore this history, we'll see how these choices echo into today, shaping challenges and opportunities that are still with us. By understanding these roots, we're not just learning about the past—we're preparing ourselves to imagine, and maybe even build, a more just future.
